content: 1. This report provides an update to the 2000 recommendations by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) regarding the use of influenza vaccines and antiviral agents. 2. The 2001 recommendations include new or revised information on the cost-effectiveness of influenza vaccination, the influenza vaccine supply, neuraminidase-inhibitor antiviral drugs, the 2001-2002 trivalent vaccine virus strains (A/Moscow/10/99 [H3N2]-like, A/New Caledonia/20/99 [H1N1]-like, and B/Sichuan/379/99-like strains), and the extension of the optimal vaccination period through November. 3. A link to this report and additional information about influenza can be accessed on the CDC's Influenza Branch website, Division of Viral and Rickettsial Diseases, National Center for Infectious Diseases. 4. The ACIP recommends strategies to improve vaccination rates, such as reminder/recall systems and standing orders programs. 5. While influenza vaccination remains the cornerstone of influenza prevention and treatment, updated information on antiviral medications is also included, as these agents serve as an adjunct to vaccination. 6. Influenza epidemics typically occur during the winter months and are responsible for an average of approximately 20,000 deaths annually in the United States. 7. Influenza viruses can also cause pandemics, during which illness and death rates from influenza-related complications can increase dramatically worldwide. 8. Influenza viruses affect individuals across all age groups, with the highest infection rates among children. However, the highest rates of severe illness and death occur among individuals aged 65 years and older and those of any age with medical conditions that increase their risk for complications. 9. Influenza vaccination is the primary method for preventing influenza and its severe complications. 10. The ACIP report identifies primary target groups for annual vaccination, including individuals at increased risk for influenza-related complications (e.g., persons aged 65 years and older, individuals with chronic medical conditions), individuals aged 50-64 years due to the higher prevalence of chronic conditions in this group, and individuals who live with or care for high-risk persons (e.g., healthcare workers and household members). 11. Vaccination is associated with reductions in influenza-related respiratory illness, physician visits across all age groups, hospitalizations and deaths among high-risk individuals, otitis media in children, and work absenteeism in adults. 12. Despite substantial increases in influenza vaccination rates, further improvements in vaccine coverage are needed, particularly among high-risk individuals under 65 years of age. 13. The 2001 recommendations include five principal changes: Added information on the cost-effectiveness of influenza vaccination. Added information on the influenza vaccine supply. Updated information on neuraminidase-inhibitor antiviral drugs. Identification of the 2001-2002 trivalent vaccine virus strains. Extension of the recommended optimal vaccination period to October-November. 14. Influenza A and B are the two types of influenza viruses that cause epidemic human disease. Influenza A viruses are further categorized into subtypes based on two surface antigens: hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). Influenza B viruses are not categorized into subtypes. 15. Since 1977, influenza A (H1N1), influenza A (H3N2), and influenza B viruses have been in global circulation. Both influenza A and B viruses are further separated into groups based on antigenic characteristics. 16. New influenza virus variants arise from frequent antigenic changes (antigenic drift) due to point mutations during viral replication. Influenza B viruses undergo antigenic drift less rapidly than influenza A viruses. 17. Immunity to surface antigens, particularly hemagglutinin, reduces the likelihood of infection and the severity of disease if infection occurs. However, antibodies against one influenza virus type or subtype provide limited or no protection against another type or subtype. 18. Frequent development of antigenic variants through antigenic drift is the virologic basis for seasonal epidemics and necessitates the inclusion of one or more new strains in each year’s influenza vaccine. 19. Influenza viruses are primarily transmitted from person to person through respiratory droplets produced by coughing and sneezing. 20. The incubation period for influenza is 1-4 days, with an average of 2 days. Individuals can be infectious from the day before symptom onset to approximately 5 days after illness onset, with children remaining infectious for longer periods. 21. Uncomplicated influenza illness is characterized by the abrupt onset of constitutional and respiratory symptoms, including fever, myalgia, headache, severe malaise, nonproductive cough, sore throat, and rhinitis. 22. Influenza-related respiratory illness is difficult to distinguish from illnesses caused by other respiratory pathogens based on symptoms alone. 23. Influenza illness typically resolves after several days for most individuals, although cough and malaise can persist for more than two weeks. 24. In some individuals, influenza can exacerbate underlying medical conditions (e.g., pulmonary or cardiac disease), lead to secondary bacterial pneumonia or primary influenza viral pneumonia, or occur as part of a co-infection with other viral or bacterial pathogens. 25. Influenza infection has also been associated with encephalopathy, transverse myelitis, Reye syndrome, myositis, myocarditis, and pericarditis. 26. The risks for complications, hospitalizations, and deaths from influenza are higher among individuals aged 65 years and older, very young children, and individuals of any age with certain underlying health conditions compared to healthy older children and younger adults. 27. Influenza vaccination is the most effective means of reducing the impact of influenza, particularly among high-risk groups. 28. Vaccination coverage can be increased by administering vaccines during hospitalizations or routine healthcare visits before the influenza season, reducing the need for special visits to physicians’ offices or clinics. 29. When vaccine and epidemic strains are well-matched, increased vaccination rates among individuals in closed settings (e.g., nursing homes) and among staff can reduce the risk of outbreaks by inducing herd immunity. 30. Vaccination of healthcare workers and others in close contact with high-risk individuals can reduce influenza transmission and subsequent influenza-related complications. 31. Influenza-specific antiviral drugs for chemoprophylaxis or treatment are an important adjunct to vaccination but are not a substitute for vaccination. 32. The influenza vaccine contains three strains (two type A and one type B) representing the viruses likely to circulate in the upcoming winter. The vaccine is made from highly purified, egg-grown viruses that have been inactivated. 33. The trivalent influenza vaccine for the 2001-2002 season includes A/Moscow/10/99 (H3N2)-like, A/New Caledonia/20/99 (H1N1)-like, and B/Sichuan/379/99-like antigens. 34. The effectiveness of the influenza vaccine depends on the age and immunocompetence of the recipient and the degree of similarity between the vaccine and circulating viruses. 35. Most vaccinated children and young adults develop high post-vaccination hemagglutination-inhibition antibody titers, which are protective against illness caused by strains similar to those in the vaccine. 36. Among healthy individuals under 65 years of age, the influenza vaccine prevents illness in approximately 70%-90% of cases when the vaccine and circulating viruses are antigenically similar. 37. Vaccination of healthy adults has been associated with decreased work absenteeism and reduced use of healthcare resources, including antibiotics, when the vaccine and circulating viruses are well-matched. 38. Among elderly individuals, the vaccine is 30%-70% effective in preventing hospitalization for pneumonia and influenza and 50%-60% effective in preventing hospitalization or pneumonia among nursing home residents. It is 80% effective in preventing death, even though its effectiveness in preventing influenza illness often ranges from 30%-40%. 39. Influenza vaccination can reduce healthcare costs and productivity losses associated with influenza illness. 40. Economic studies have demonstrated cost savings and substantial reductions in hospitalizations and deaths among individuals aged 65 years and older. 41. Increasing vaccination coverage among high-risk individuals under 65 years of age, including children, is a high priority for expanding influenza vaccine use. 42. Annual vaccination is recommended for healthcare workers, but vaccination rates among this group remain suboptimal. 43. Limited information is available regarding influenza vaccine use among pregnant women, despite evidence of increased risk for influenza-related morbidity and mortality during the last two trimesters of pregnancy. 44. Influenza vaccine is strongly recommended for individuals aged six months and older who are at increased risk for complications due to age or underlying medical conditions. 45. Vaccination is also recommended for healthcare workers and individuals in close contact with high-risk persons to reduce the risk of transmission.
